newsitem.title: USA: Marketing to teens has pitfalls and promise.
newsitem.headline: Marketing to teens has pitfalls and promise.

text.p: Take any shopping mall across the broad land. Teen clothing stores are sprouting everywhere, filling the vacuum created by a wave of store closings in other sectors.
But it's not just clothes for teens that is booming. It's also books, electronics, music, cosmetics sporting goods, bicycles and related equipment.
And more.
By almost any measure, American teenagers are turning into conspicuous consumers.
"The minimum-wage hike will provide a significant boost in teen earnings," predicts Maria Medaris O'Shea, analyst at Alex Brown & Sons, a Baltimore investment house.

"We estimate aggregate teen earnings will rise 6 percent, 14 percent and 8 percent in 1996, 1997 and 1998, respectively, based purely on the increased wages and overall growth in the teen population."

Beyond "teens' great economic power," she says, "we are in the early stage of an 18-year teen demographic wave." In 1992, teenage Americans had their first population increase after 15 years of annual declines, she said.
"With a total of 14 years of annual teen population increases ahead of us, the teen population should peak in 2009 at over 30 million, breaking the previous record of 29.5 million teens set in 1976."
Lured by the lush prospects, consumer goods producers, retailers, advertising agencies and marketers are scrambling to get their share of the teen pie.
But there are pitfalls, some believe, and more than a few consumer-goods sellers already have fallen into them.

"You have to be careful," warns Jill Kossoff, senior brand planner for J. Walter Thompson, the New York advertising agency. "There's a lot of spending power out there, but too many trying to sell the teens are talking down to them, ignoring the fact that teenagers today are cynical and don't want to be condescended to."

"The main hurdle in marketing to teens is to create an enduring brand that has power for them but which plays a role in letting them find themselves," asserts Lynn Fischer, vice president and a research director for Young & Rubicam, the New York advertising agency.
"It has to rise above the trends of today and offer them the option for individuality," Fischer said.

The road is littered with failed teen magazines and cosmetics that have failed to heed that advice. Conversely, there are the products and companies that have intrigued teen customers and turned them into loyal fans. They include Nike athletic shoes, Levi jeans, Dr. Pepper beverages, Kodak's new advanced photo system and Trident chewing gum.

As everyone knows by now, teens are tricky customers because they want to be both individuals and yet conform with their peers. Kossoff, of the Thompson agency, says teenagers see themselves dealing with big problems like air and water -pollution, a huge national deficit, difficulties finding jobs even after college "and that has made them want to live for today and not think of what's ahead."

So, anything with new technology works for them because "it does things for me and lets me express myself." she said. But it must be new. "Pagers, beepers, cellular phones are hot. Walkmans and compact disks are cold -- part of the past."
Even those who succeed at winning the teen audience can't rest on their laurels. As a teen-loved brand evolves, the approach has to change if it is to remain viable.
"The marketing communications must vary as the teen customer changes," says Fischer of Young & Rubicam.

Snapple is a good example of a brand that didn't change, she suggests. "The Snapple people did a good job, communicating clearly to the teens who gave the product a great word-of-mouth and made it a leading-edge-product," said Fischer.

But after that burst of business, Snapple did not know how to cope with the next stage of going more mainstream. By contrast, Dr. Pepper has done a better job, letting the teen customer feel like individuals but also as part of a social group," she said. Dr. Pepper is a Young & Rubicam client.
So, the teens, it must be concluded, are slippery customers. One source cited the example of a cosmetics producer who went after the young market with a facial palette of five shades.
Wasn't that enough choice for the teens? "No," came the reply. "The palette should have been open-ended."
Open-ended? How many shades does it take to be "open-ended?" Anyone one who knows the answer and can put it cost-effectively on the market will surely make scads of money.
